actually then seized the keys to the office and locked himself inside. In 
February 1868, Johnson formally removed Stanton as war secretary. The 
House impeached Johnson three days later for violating the Tenure in 
Office Act, and a Senate trial duly followed. Johnson escaped conviction by 
a single vote, thus arguably ratifying Johnson’s constitutional stance, at 
least with regard to a president’s war secretary.
The 1867 Act remained on the books until its repeal by the Act of 
March 3, 1887, ch. 353, 24 Stat. 500. That development hardly terminated, 
however, the ongoing pohtical debate about the scope of presidential 
removal power. Just a month earlier. Congress had created what is 
generally considered the first modern regulatory commission, the 
Interstate Commerce Commission. Act of Feb. 4, 1887, ch. 104, 24 Stat. 
379. That Act provided that the president could remove any of the new 
commission’s five members for “inefficiency, neglect of duty, or malfeasance 
in office.” Id. at 383. Moreover, Congress’s 1887 repeal of the Tenure in 
Office Act left in place provisions of the 1876 Postal Services 
Appropriations Act, Act of July 12, 1876, Ch. 179, 19 Stat. 80, 81, which 
provided: ‘Postmasters of the first, second, and third classes shall be 
appointed and may be removed by the President by and with the advice 
and consent of the Senate, and shall hold their offices for four years unless 
sooner removed or suspended according to law.” President Wilson’s 1920 
discharge of a first-class postmaster without Senate consent gave the 
Supreme Court its first opportunity to opine definitively on the scope of 
presidential removal power.

This case presents the question whether under the Constitution the 
President has the exclusive power of removing executive officers of the 
United States whom he has appointed by and with the advice and consent 
of the Senate. * * *
It is very clear from [the] history [of the Decision of 1789] that the

recognize and declare the power of the President under the Constitution to 
remove the Secretary of Foreign Affairs without the advice and consent of 
the Senate. That was what the vote was taken for. Some effort has been
